strengths: Novel optical system combining chromatic focal sweep with simple off-the-shelf lenses and grayscale sensor, making hyperspectral imaging more practical and accessible
Comprehensive experimental validation including synthetic data on 30 Harvard images, comparisons with 6 state-of-the-art methods, and real prototype demonstrations
Achieves competitive performance (24.10 dB PSNR) with only 4 optical components while maintaining fast reconstruction (<1 second), addressing practical constraints of existing hyperspectral systems
Well-designed presentation with clear optical design diagrams and effective result visualizations across diverse scenes
Physics-based computational approach grounded in forward imaging model, providing interpretability beyond pure deep learning methods
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty - plug-and-play ADMM is well-established; once the forward model is defined, the reconstruction is relatively standard with no ablation studies on component contributions
Insufficient reproducibility details: the critical deep learning denoiser is only described as 'off-the-shelf' without specifying architecture, training data, or which pretrained network is used
Modest performance gains over strong baseline: KRISM achieves 21.12 dB PSNR/0.38 SAM compared to this work's 24.10 dB/0.61 SAM - the 3 dB improvement comes with worse spectral accuracy (higher SAM)
Limited real-world validation with only one prototype camera tested on few scenes; Figure 6 shows color artifacts (false colors in grayscale patterns) indicating practical limitations not addressed

Incomplete technical analysis: no systematic study of how measurement count N affects reconstruction quality, no characterization of chromatic aberration magnitude, and lens choice appears empirically driven without justification
Acknowledged performance degradation at longer wavelengths (>600nm) and missing details on exact wavelength coverage and spectral resolution capabilities

Reproducibility concerns: forward model assumes perfect linear imaging despite real optical aberrations, ADMM hyperparameter choices not justified, GitHub code/data availability claimed but not specified
Small test set (30 images) with simulated conditions; evaluation assumes uniform brightness and specific Poisson noise statistics without exploring robustness to realistic lighting variation

strengths: Novel optical design exploiting chromatic aberration for spectral imaging with only 4 optical components vs. 20+ in competitors
Clear physics-based mathematical formulation with explicit optical forward model and interpretable optimization framework
Demonstration of working hardware prototype with proper experimental setup and calibration
Reasonable technical execution of the algorithm with proper ADMM derivation and fast matrix inversion via BCCB structure
Comprehensive comparison against multiple SOTA methods (KRISM, MST, CASSI variants) in simulated experiments
weaknesses: Severely limited evaluation scope: only 30 images for simulated experiments and trivial custom scenes (color checkers, toys) for real data validation—far below CVPR standards
Unsubstantiated 'state-of-the-art' claims: no quantitative real-world comparison with other methods, only visual comparisons; KRISM actually outperforms SfD in SAM (34.38 vs 36.51) in Table 1
Modest quantitative improvements that don't justify complexity: PSNR improvements ~3 dB over MST/KRISM, SSIM gains are marginal (~0.08)

Critical practical limitations not adequately addressed: shallow depth of field (34 cm), wavelength range restricted to 463-610 nm with visible degradation beyond 600 nm (Figure 6), requiring precise optical calibration
Visible quality issues in real data results: spatial and spectral artifacts evident in Figures 4-6, false color patterns and blurring in reconstructed images, especially at longer wavelengths

Contradictory claims about 'physics-based interpretability': heavy reliance on pre-trained off-the-shelf deep learning denoiser φ_θ undermines interpretability and limits generalization; no ablation study of denoiser contribution
Misleading 'fast' computation claim: <1 second conflates capture time with reconstruction time; actual computational cost vs. other iterative methods not clearly reported or compared

Missing ablation studies and sensitivity analysis: no investigation of regularization parameters, denoiser impact, number of measurements N, algorithm convergence properties, or initialization sensitivity
Reproducibility concerns: custom prototype prevents easy replication, detailed optical calibration procedures not provided, denoiser training details minimal, no code release mentioned

strengths: Novel and elegant optical approach: Cleverly exploits chromatic focal aberration as a sensing mechanism rather than treating it as a limitation
Practical hardware prototype with real data validation: Authors built and demonstrated an actual camera, providing experimental evidence beyond simulations
State-of-the-art performance: Achieves 24.10 dB PSNR and 0.61 SSIM, outperforming established methods (TF, SDC, MST, KRISM, etc.) while using far fewer optical components (4 vs 9-20)
Remarkable simplicity and practicality: Extremely compact design using off-the-shelf optics, enabling low cost and easy deployment
Sound technical methodology: Well-motivated physics-based forward model combined with modern optimization (ADMM with plug-and-play deep learning denoiser)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Tests on multiple synthetic datasets (KAIST, CAVE) and real data with diverse metrics (PSNR, SSIM, SAM, ΔE₀₀)
Clear and well-motivated presentation: Effectively articulates limitations of existing approaches and clearly explains how the proposed method addresses them with good visual explanations
Fast reconstruction: Achieves hyperspectral image recovery in <1 second, practical for real-time applications
weaknesses: Limited real-world data evaluation: Real experiments focus on controlled setups (Macbeth chart, static objects); more diverse natural scenes and challenging conditions would strengthen practical claims
Incomplete computational comparisons: Lacks detailed timing comparisons with competing methods across different resolutions and hardware configurations
Hardware reproducibility concerns: Custom optical prototype with specific lens mounts and mechanisms may be difficult for others to replicate; code availability not mentioned
Missing ablation studies: Limited analysis of key design choices such as optimal number of lens positions N, denoiser selection, and regularization parameter sensitivity
Wavelength coverage limitations: Evaluation restricted to visible spectrum; applicability to near-IR, UV, or other wavelength ranges not explored
Insufficient failure mode analysis: Limited discussion of performance degradation scenarios (low-light conditions, optical misalignment, system-specific sensitivity)
Generalization across optical systems unclear: Unclear whether reconstruction algorithm requires system-specific calibration or how it transfers to different optical configurations
Limited noise robustness analysis: While Poisson noise is simulated, systematic evaluation across SNR levels and real noise characteristics would be valuable

strengths: Novel hardware design: Creative exploitation of chromatic aberration to encode spectral information using only two off-the-shelf lenses and a grayscale sensor significantly reduces optical complexity compared to existing systems
Well-motivated technical approach: Physics-based forward model (Eq. 1) is correctly formulated, and plug-and-play ADMM algorithm (Eq. 3) properly combines physical constraints with learned priors
Comprehensive simulation results: Extensive evaluation on KAIST and CAVE datasets with systematic comparison against 9 competing methods demonstrates SOTA PSNR (30.81 dB) and strong SSIM/SAM metrics
Working hardware prototype: Real optical system with Liquid Crystal Tunable Filters demonstrates feasibility and validates simulation results
Clear presentation: Paper is well-written with effective motivation, clear mathematical exposition, and informative figures illustrating the concept and reconstruction quality
Practical system design: Thoughtful consideration of practical aspects including PSF calibration, grayscale sensor utilization, and explicit magnification modeling
weaknesses: Severely limited real-world validation: Real hardware results are minimal (Section 4.4) with no quantitative metrics (PSNR/SSIM) reported on actual captured images, only brief visual comparisons. This critically weakens a paper claiming to present a working system. Complete absence of comparison with competing methods on real data.

Narrow working range severely limits applicability: System requires ~34 cm working range with rapid degradation beyond ~29 cm (Figure 5). This represents only ~8.5 cm error tolerance. Paper documents but does not address this fundamental limitation or propose solutions, leaving practical deployment ambiguous.

Limited spectral flexibility: Coverage restricted to visible spectrum (400-720 nm) determined by fixed lens aberration characteristics. Non-uniform wavelength sampling not analyzed. System cannot adaptively select wavelengths and is specific to chosen lens pair.

Missing critical ablation and sensitivity studies: No ablation studies on algorithm components (regularization weight λ, dual variables μ₁, μ₂), no hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, no justification for hyperparameter choices, no convergence guarantees for Algorithm 1, and no analysis of calibration error sensitivity

Algorithm novelty limited: Plug-and-play ADMM framework comes from prior work [10]. Application is straightforward instantiation using off-the-shelf deep denoiser, limiting algorithmic contribution beyond the hardware design

Incomplete implementation details: Calibration procedure not detailed (number of measurements, fitting method unclear). Critical algorithm details relegated to supplementary material. Computational complexity and runtime analysis entirely missing

Narrow experimental evaluation scope: Only two standard datasets evaluated. Simulation assumes ideal Poisson noise while real sensors may differ. No evaluation on other public hyperspectral benchmarks (Indian Pines, Salinas, etc.). Comparison mainly with academic methods, not commercial systems

Missing temporal and practical analysis: No discussion of multi-frame requirements or temporal resolution. No analysis of how many focal positions N are needed for good reconstruction. No runtime or computational cost analysis. Target applications not discussed
Unvalidated assumptions: Claim that magnification remains constant across focal stack (Sec 3.1) lacks experimental verification. Relationship between PSF and focal position could be more explicit

strengths: Practical and affordable hardware design using only off-the-shelf components (two lenses + grayscale sensor), with actual prototype construction and real data collection
Well-motivated physics-based forward model leveraging chromatic aberration as natural wavelength separator, avoiding complex custom optics
Comprehensive systematic comparison with 9 SOTA methods across multiple metrics (PSNR, SSIM, SAM, computational cost, optical requirements)
Solid experimental methodology with realistic noise models accounting for photon efficiency in simulations
Competitive simulated performance results (PSNR 30.81 dB, SSIM 0.92) achieving state-of-the-art quality on KAIST and CAVE datasets
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: core reconstruction uses standard plug-and-play ADMM with off-the-shelf denoisers; adaptation to this problem is straightforward application of existing techniques without significant innovation

Severe practical limitations inadequately addressed: (1) Only ~29 spectral bands at 20nm intervals vs 150+ for true HSI systems; (2) Working range limited to 34cm depth; (3) Cannot capture dynamic scenes requiring sequential lens positioning; (4) 5-second exposure time impractical for real-world use

Clear failure cases in real data undermine robustness claims: pinwheel test shows complete inability to reconstruct fine patterns; low-exposure performance exhibits severe hallucinations; spectral reconstruction fails for black/dark regions

Incomplete real-world validation: only 4-5 test scenes; ground truth limited to Macbeth patches; no full-scene spectral accuracy metrics; gap between simulated and real performance not adequately explained

Insufficient experimental analysis: no ablations on component contributions (physics vs learning); missing comparisons with recent learning-based methods; limited evaluation breadth (only KAIST/CAVE datasets); no analysis of reconstruction quality vs measurement trade-offs

Questionable gap between claims and evidence: title promises 'state-of-the-art hyperspectral imaging' but spectral coverage (visible only) and resolution fall short of true HSI systems; 'robust' performance contradicted by failures under noise and challenging lighting

Reproducibility concerns: precise mechanical calibration and lens positioning difficult to replicate; denoiser training details underspecified; PSF calibration procedure lacks sufficient technical detail

Missing critical analyses: no convergence guarantees for plug-and-play ADMM with learned components; hyperparameter selection process not justified; insufficient exploration of failure modes and model assumptions under extreme conditions

Well-motivated physics-based plus data-driven hybrid approach combining forward modeling with plug-and-play ADMM and deep learning regularization for both interpretability and performance
Comprehensive experimental validation including extensive simulations on KAIST/CAVE datasets, working prototype implementation, real-world data collection, and robustness studies
Clear and well-organized presentation with informative figures effectively illustrating the optical design, system architecture, and comparative results
Honest and transparent discussion of limitations and failure modes, demonstrating technical maturity and research integrity
weaknesses: Inherent working range limitations (~34 cm depth of field) that may constrain applicability in dynamic scenes, despite demonstrated robustness beyond theoretical predictions
Real-world performance challenges including sensor noise artifacts in dark regions, inability to reconstruct fine spectral patterns, and spectral accuracy issues for certain object types

Insufficient analysis of deep learning regularizer generalization across different scene types, noise characteristics, and imaging conditions
